blurb: The rules being written for AI: Europe's AI Act, how the US, China and UK differ, the copyright fights, and laws that affect you.

steps.h: The world's first big AI law
steps.p: The European Union's AI Act, agreed in 2024, sorts AI uses by how much harm they could do, with stricter rules for riskier uses.
Uses like government "social scoring" of citizens, and manipulative AI that exploits vulnerable people.
AI used in hiring, credit scoring, schools or policing must meet requirements on data quality, human oversight and documentation.
Chatbots must make clear you're talking to a machine, and AI-generated deepfakes must be labelled.
Any company offering AI to people in the EU must comply, wherever it's based — so it shapes products worldwide.
steps.analogy: Like EU phone-charger rules leading to USB-C on iPhones everywhere.

cards.q: Which practice does the EU AI Act ban outright?
cards.hint: The top of the risk ladder.
cards.why: Social scoring. Ranking citizens by behaviour to grant or deny opportunities is considered an unacceptable risk.

cards.statement: The EU AI Act applies only to companies based in the EU.
cards.why: False. It applies to anyone offering AI systems to people in the EU — including US and Chinese companies.

cards.q: The maximum fine for using a banned AI practice is…
options: Up to €35 million or 7% of global annual turnover
cards.why: €35M or 7% of turnover, whichever is higher. For a giant company, 7% of worldwide revenue is enormous.

cards.title: The EU's bans on prohibited AI practices took effect on 2 February 2025.
cards.detail: Rules for makers of general-purpose AI models followed on 2 August 2025, with most high-risk rules scheduled for later years.

cards.statement: Under the EU AI Act, chatbots must make clear people are talking to an AI.
cards.why: True. It's one of the transparency rules — you have the right to know you're not chatting with a person.

steps.p: No single national AI law. Policy shifts with each president, and states like California and Colorado write their own rules.
Detailed rules for specific technologies — recommendation feeds, deepfakes, chatbots — including content controls and registering services with regulators.
Lets existing regulators (for finance, health, etc.) apply principles in their areas, and set up an institute to test frontier AI.
Each reflects its politics: markets, state control, or flexibility.
Countries cooperate through summits and reports, but there's no single binding global treaty covering all AI.
steps.analogy: Like driving: every country has road rules, but they differ — and you follow the local ones.

cards.q: What happened to President Biden's 2023 executive order on AI?
options: It was copied by the EU
cards.hint: US policy shifts with each president.
cards.why: Revoked. The incoming administration replaced it with policy focused on reducing barriers to AI development.

cards.statement: China requires public generative AI services to follow content rules and file with regulators.
cards.why: True. Its 2023 rules require outputs to align with official values and services to register their algorithms.

cards.q: In February 2025, the UK's AI Safety Institute was renamed the…
cards.why: AI Security Institute. The new name signalled more focus on security threats like cyberattacks and weapons misuse.

cards.title: California's governor vetoed a major AI safety bill in 2024, then signed a narrower one in 2025.
cards.detail: SB 1047, which would have imposed liability-linked safety duties, was vetoed. SB 53, signed in September 2025, instead requires large AI developers to publish safety frameworks and report serious incidents.

cards.statement: A single global treaty binds every country to the same AI rules.
cards.why: False. There are agreements and declarations, but no binding worldwide rulebook. Rules differ a lot by country.

steps.p: AI models learn from huge amounts of books, articles, art and music — much of it copyrighted. Is that allowed without permission?
US law allows some uses without permission. Judges weigh four factors, including whether the use transforms the work and whether it hurts the original's market.
Authors, news outlets, artists and record labels have sued AI companies, arguing training copied their work unfairly.
In 2025 one judge said training on lawfully bought books was fair use, but keeping pirated copies was not. Another found copying legal summaries for a competing tool wasn't fair use.
steps.analogy: Learning from library books you borrowed is different from photocopying stolen ones.

steps.p: In the US, work made entirely by AI with no human creative input can't be copyrighted. Human choices and edits can be.

cards.q: In 2025, a US judge in the Bartz v. Anthropic case ruled that…
options: Training on lawfully acquired books was fair use, but keeping pirated copies was not
Authors must be paid per word
cards.why: A split decision. Learning from books was transformative; storing pirated copies was not. Anthropic later settled with the authors.

cards.statement: In the US, a work generated entirely by AI with no human authorship cannot be copyrighted.
cards.why: True. The US Copyright Office and courts require human authorship. Human selection and editing of AI output can still be protected.

cards.q: Which fair-use factor asks whether AI outputs replace the original works?
options: The effect on the market for the original
cards.why: Market effect. If AI outputs substitute for buying the original, that weighs against fair use.

cards.title: The New York Times sued OpenAI and Microsoft in December 2023 over the use of its articles in training.
cards.detail: It alleged millions of articles were used without permission and showed models reproducing passages nearly word for word.

cards.statement: A 2025 US ruling found that using Westlaw legal summaries to train a competing AI tool was not fair use.
cards.why: True. In Thomson Reuters v. Ross, the judge said the use wasn't transformative and competed with the original — a different result from the book cases.

steps.p: Privacy laws like Europe's GDPR give you rights over personal data — including data used by AI. Regulators have challenged chatbots over it.
AI trained on past decisions can copy past bias. Hiring, lending and housing AI faces growing rules on testing for discrimination.
Some places now require bias audits for AI hiring tools and that candidates be told when AI is used.
New laws target fake intimate images and election deepfakes, and require platforms to remove them quickly.
Many employers have rules about which AI tools you may use and what data you can paste in.
steps.analogy: Like rules about forwarding work emails to your personal account.

cards.q: Why did Italy's data protection authority temporarily block ChatGPT in 2023?
options: Concerns about personal data processing and age checks
cards.why: Privacy concerns. OpenAI added privacy controls and age checks, and service returned within about a month.

cards.statement: Amazon scrapped an experimental AI recruiting tool after it learned to mark down applications mentioning the word "women's".
cards.hint: Look at the flow in step 2.
cards.why: True. Trained on a decade of mostly male hires, it learned the bias. Amazon dropped it, reported Reuters in 2018.

cards.q: New York City's Local Law 144 requires employers using automated hiring tools to…
options: Get an annual bias audit and tell candidates
cards.why: Audit and notify. It was one of the first laws requiring bias checks for AI hiring tools.

cards.title: The US TAKE IT DOWN Act, signed in 2025, criminalises publishing non-consensual intimate images — including AI deepfakes.
cards.detail: It also requires platforms to remove such content within 48 hours of a valid request from the person shown.

cards.title: Know your workplace's AI rules
cards.body: Pasting confidential data into a public chatbot can break company policy or privacy law.
cards.challenge: Find out whether your workplace or school has an AI policy, and what it says about sharing data.
